# MCP Protocol Server



The BioKernel MCP (Model Context Protocol) Server is the stdio-based JSON-RPC 2.0 gateway that makes the entire biomedical skills catalog discoverable and executable from any MCP-compatible client — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, and beyond. Rather than building a proprietary API surface, the platform speaks the open MCP specification (version `2024-11-05`), turning 59+ biomedical skill domains into first-class tools that LLM clients can list, route, invoke, and chain without custom integration code. This page explains the server's architecture, its four exposed tools, the request lifecycle from JSON-RPC message to skill execution, and how it connects to the broader BioKernel engine.

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L1-L18), [server.py](biokernel/biokernel/server.py#L1-L16)

## Protocol Foundation and Transport

The MCP server communicates over **stdio** (stdin/stdout) using newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 messages. This transport choice is deliberate: stdio is the MCP specification's canonical local transport, requiring no network ports, no CORS configuration, and no firewall rules. The client launches the server as a subprocess, writes JSON-RPC requests to its stdin, and reads responses from its stdout. All diagnostic logging is redirected to stderr to avoid corrupting the protocol stream — a critical design constraint enforced at initialization time.

The protocol handshake follows the MCP lifecycle: the client sends an `initialize` request, the server responds with its protocol version and capabilities, the client sends a `notifications/initialized` notification, and the connection is ready for tool discovery and invocation. The server declares both `tools` and `prompts` capabilities, meaning clients can enumerate executable tools *and* retrieve pre-built prompt templates derived from registered SKILL.md files.

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L145-L200), [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L30-L37)

## Architecture: MCP Server Within the BioKernel

The MCP server is not a standalone application — it is a thin protocol adapter that delegates all business logic to the `BioKernel` core engine. Understanding this layering is essential for working with the system effectively.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph MCP_Client["MCP-Compatible Client"]
        C[Claude Desktop / Cursor / Claude Code]
    end

    subgraph Transport["Stdio Transport"]
        STDIN["stdin ← JSON-RPC requests"]
        STDOUT["stdout → JSON-RPC responses"]
        STDERR["stderr → diagnostic logs"]
    end

    subgraph MCPServer["MCPServer (biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py)"]
        INIT["initialize / notifications"]
        TOOLS_LIST["tools/list"]
        TOOLS_CALL["tools/call"]
        PROMPTS["prompts/list & prompts/get"]
    end

    subgraph BioKernel["BioKernel Core Engine"]
        ROUTER["SkillRouter<br/>TF-IDF semantic routing"]
        EXEC["execute()<br/>Route → Prompt → LLM"]
        WF["WorkflowEngine<br/>DAG orchestration"]
        PROV["LLM Providers<br/>Anthropic / OpenAI / Gemini / Local"]
    end

    C -->|writes| STDIN
    STDOUT -->|reads| C
    STDERR -.->|logs| C

    STDIN --> MCPServer
    MCPServer -->|delegates| BioKernel
    TOOLS_CALL -->|run_bio_agent| EXEC
    TOOLS_CALL -->|list_skills| ROUTER
    TOOLS_CALL -->|route_query| ROUTER
    TOOLS_CALL -->|run_workflow| WF
    EXEC --> ROUTER
    EXEC --> PROV
    WF --> EXEC
    PROMPTS -->|skill instructions| ROUTER
```

When the `MCPServer` class instantiates, it creates a `BioKernel` instance by loading configuration from `config.yaml` (or environment overrides). The BioKernel then initializes the `SkillRouter`, the `WorkflowEngine`, and all configured LLM providers, and discovers skills from the filesystem. The MCP server holds this kernel as `self.kernel` and routes every incoming `tools/call` request to the appropriate kernel method. This separation means the MCP server contains zero domain logic — it is purely a serialization and dispatch layer.

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L145-L156), [server.py](biokernel/biokernel/server.py#L74-L115), [config.yaml](biokernel/config.yaml#L1-L76)

## The Four Exposed Tools

The server registers exactly four tools in its `tools/list` response. Each tool maps to a distinct capability within the BioKernel, and together they cover the full lifecycle from discovery to execution to multi-step orchestration.

| Tool | Purpose | Required Params | Optional Params | Returns |
|------|---------|-----------------|-----------------|---------|
| **`run_bio_agent`** | Execute a biomedical skill via natural language query | `query` | `skill_id`, `provider` | Response text + metadata (skill used, provider, model, timing, safety flags) |
| **`list_skills`** | Discover all registered skills with descriptions | — | `category` | Markdown-formatted skill catalog |
| **`route_query`** | Preview skill routing without execution | `query` | — | Ranked skill matches with similarity scores |
| **`run_workflow`** | Execute a multi-step DAG workflow | `name`, `steps[]` | — | Workflow status with per-step results and total latency |

### `run_bio_agent` — The Primary Execution Tool

This is the workhorse tool. When an MCP client sends a natural-language biomedical query, `run_bio_agent` constructs an `AgentRequest`, optionally overrides the skill routing with an explicit `skill_id` or the LLM `provider` preference, and delegates to `BioKernel.execute()`. The kernel then routes the query to the best-matching skill via TF-IDF semantic similarity, builds a context-aware system prompt from the skill's metadata and instructions body, sends the prompt to the selected LLM provider, runs safety checks on the output, and returns a structured `AgentResponse`. The MCP tool wraps this response into the standard MCP content format, attaching execution metadata (skill used, provider, model, timing, safety flags) so the client can audit what happened.

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L44-L138), [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L247-L267)

### `list_skills` — Skill Discovery

The `list_skills` tool provides a zero-side-effect way to browse the catalog. It calls `BioKernel.list_skills()`, which iterates over all skills registered in the `SkillRouter` and returns their `skill_id`, name, description, type, category, and tags. An optional `category` filter narrows results by matching against the skill's category field or tags. The output is formatted as Markdown, making it immediately readable in chat-based MCP clients.

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L269-L285), [server.py](biokernel/biokernel/server.py#L401-L413)

### `route_query` — Dry-Run Routing

Before committing to execution, a client can call `route_query` to see which skills would match a given query and how strongly. This invokes `SkillRouter.route()` with `top_k=5`, returning up to five matches with their cosine similarity scores. The threshold is configurable (default `0.35` in `config.yaml`). This tool is valuable for debugging routing behavior, exploring the skill catalog interactively, or building approval workflows where a human reviews the proposed skill before execution.

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L287-L299), [router.py](biokernel/biokernel/router.py#L56-L96)

### `run_workflow` — Multi-Step DAG Orchestration

The most complex tool, `run_workflow`, accepts a workflow name and an array of steps. Each step specifies a `step_id`, a `skill_id`, an optional `depends_on` list (referencing other step IDs), and an optional `query`. The tool converts these into a `WorkflowDefinition` and delegates to `BioKernel.execute_workflow()`, which uses the DAG-based `WorkflowEngine` to execute steps in topological order with automatic parallelization of independent steps. Upstream step results are injected as context into downstream steps. The response includes per-step status icons (✓/✗), truncated results, and total workflow latency.

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L301-L331), [server.py](biokernel/biokernel/server.py#L316-L344), [workflow_engine.py](biokernel/biokernel/workflow_engine.py#L65-L176)

## Request Lifecycle: From JSON-RPC to Skill Execution

The following flowchart traces a single `run_bio_agent` call from the moment the client writes a JSON-RPC message to the moment the response appears on stdout.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Client writes JSON-RPC<br/>tools/call → run_bio_agent"] --> B["MCPServer.handle_message()<br/>dispatch by method"]
    B --> C["_handle_tools_call()<br/>dispatch by tool name"]
    C --> D["_tool_run_agent()<br/>build AgentRequest"]
    D --> E["BioKernel.execute()<br/>1. Route query"]
    E --> F["SkillRouter.get_best_match()<br/>TF-IDF cosine similarity"]
    F --> G["BioKernel.execute()<br/>2. Build system prompt"]
    G --> H["BioKernel.execute()<br/>3. Call LLM provider"]
    H --> I["Safety checks<br/>danger terms + disclaimer"]
    I --> J["Return AgentResponse<br/>→ wrap in MCP content"]
    J --> K["JSON-RPC response<br/>written to stdout"]
```

Each step in this pipeline is observable through the stderr log stream (prefixed `[MCP:BioKernel]`), and the response metadata provides a post-hoc audit trail of which skill was selected, which provider and model were used, and whether any safety flags were raised.

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L158-L188), [server.py](biokernel/biokernel/server.py#L254-L314)

## Message Dispatch and Error Handling

The `handle_message()` method implements a clean dispatch table pattern, mapping method strings to async handler functions. When a method is not found in the dispatch table, the server returns a standard JSON-RPC error with code `-32601`. When a handler raises an exception, the server catches it and returns a `-32000` error with the exception message. Notifications (messages without an `id` field) are handled but elicit no response, conforming to the JSON-RPC specification. This design ensures that no malformed request can crash the server loop — errors are always serialized back to the client.

| JSON-RPC Method | Handler | Response Required |
|-----------------|---------|-------------------|
| `initialize` | `_handle_initialize` | Yes — returns protocol version, capabilities, server info |
| `notifications/initialized` | `_handle_notification` | No — notification only |
| `tools/list` | `_handle_tools_list` | Yes — returns the four-tool catalog |
| `tools/call` | `_handle_tools_call` | Yes — dispatches to tool implementation |
| `prompts/list` | `_handle_prompts_list` | Yes — returns skill prompts from SKILL.md files |
| `prompts/get` | `_handle_prompts_get` | Yes — returns skill instructions as prompt messages |
| *(any other)* | `None` | Yes — returns error code `-32601` |

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L158-L188), [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L335-L341)

## Prompts Capability: SKILL.md as Prompt Templates

Beyond tools, the MCP server exposes a **prompts** capability. When a client calls `prompts/list`, the server iterates over all registered skills of type `skill_md` and returns each as a named prompt with its description. When `prompts/get` is called with a specific skill name, the server retrieves that skill's `instructions_body` — the parsed Markdown content from the SKILL.md file below the YAML frontmatter — and wraps it as a user message in the MCP prompt format. This allows MCP clients to inject domain-specific biomedical instructions into their conversation context without executing a skill, enabling patterns like "load the oncology skill instructions as context, then answer my question."

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L220-L243), [server.py](biokernel/biokernel/server.py#L200-L250)

## The Stdio Event Loop

The server's `run()` method implements a robust async event loop over stdio. It connects `asyncio.StreamReader` to stdin and a write transport to stdout, then enters an infinite loop: read a line, parse it as JSON, dispatch to `handle_message()`, and if a response is produced, serialize it to JSON and write it to stdout with a trailing newline. The loop handles `JSONDecodeError` gracefully (logging to stderr and continuing) and exits cleanly on EOF or `KeyboardInterrupt`. This design is production-ready for long-running processes managed by MCP clients.

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L345-L391)

## Domain-Specific MCP Servers in the Skills Catalog

In addition to the core BioKernel MCP server, the platform includes specialized MCP servers registered as skills under `Skills/MCP_Servers/`. These are standalone servers that expose specific biomedical data sources as MCP tools, and they can run alongside or independently of the BioKernel server.

| Server | Location | Key Tools | Data Sources |
|--------|----------|-----------|--------------|
| **BioMCP** | `Skills/MCP_Servers/BioMCP/` | PubMed/PMC search, PubTator3 annotations, ClinicalTrials.gov, genomic variants | PubMed, PMC, PubTator3, ClinicalTrials.gov |
| **BioMCP Reference** | `Skills/MCP_Servers/BioMCP_Reference/` | `search_pubmed`, `get_gene_info` | Mock PubMed, gene database (TP53, BRCA1, EGFR) |
| **MCPmed** | `Skills/MCP_Servers/MCPmed/` | GEO integration, STRING DB, UCSC Cell Browser | GEO, STRING, UCSC Cell Browser |

The BioMCP Reference server is particularly instructive as a minimal working example — it implements the same JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio protocol with `initialize`, `tools/list`, and `tools/call` handlers in under 170 lines of Python, demonstrating how straightforward it is to wrap any biomedical API as an MCP tool.

Sources: [Skills/MCP_Servers/README.md](Skills/MCP_Servers/README.md#L1-L36), [bio_mcp_server.py](Skills/MCP_Servers/BioMCP/bio_mcp_server.py#L1-L77), [server.py (Reference)](Skills/MCP_Servers/BioMCP_Reference/server.py#L1-L173), [MCPmed SKILL.md](Skills/MCP_Servers/MCPmed/SKILL.md#L1-L57)

## MCP Operations and Security Considerations

The `MCP_Operations_2026` skill codifies the platform's operational standards for running MCP safely in production. The key decisions documented there — and enforced in the BioKernel MCP server — are:

- **Transport**: stdio for local deployments (default), Streamable HTTP for remote deployments, SSE only for backward compatibility
- **Authorization**: Explicit approval required for sensitive actions by default; per-server allowlists for tools, domains, and scopes
- **Egress**: Restrict outbound access; block private-address abuse; do not trust redirect targets or OAuth discovery endpoints blindly
- **Audit**: Log every tool import and call; the BioKernel MCP server logs all handler errors and routing decisions to stderr
- **Registry hygiene**: Prefer official or registry-listed servers over community clones; document which data sources are enabled per deployment

The BioKernel's built-in safety checks in `server.py` complement these operational controls by scanning generated output for dangerous content (e.g., "synthesize," "self-medicate") and verifying that clinical responses include appropriate disclaimers. Safety flags are returned as part of every `run_bio_agent` response metadata.

> [!TIP]
> When deploying the MCP server in a clinical environment, ensure the `enable_safety_checks: true` flag is set in `config.yaml` (it defaults to true) and that the `system.log_json: true` option is enabled for structured audit logging. The safety check system flags responses containing clinical terms (diagnosis, treatment, prescribe, medication, dosage) that lack disclaimer language (consult, healthcare, physician), returning a `safety:missing_clinical_disclaimer` flag that MCP clients can surface to users.

Sources: [MCP_Operations_2026 SKILL.md](Skills/MCP_Servers/MCP_Operations_2026/SKILL.md#L1-L51), [server.py](biokernel/biokernel/server.py#L373-L397), [config.yaml](biokernel/config.yaml#L49-L56)

## Configuration Reference

The MCP server inherits all configuration from the BioKernel's `config.yaml`. The following parameters most directly affect MCP behavior:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `default_provider` | `anthropic` | Fallback LLM provider when client doesn't specify |
| `routing.similarity_threshold` | `0.35` | Minimum cosine similarity for skill routing matches |
| `routing.fallback_skill` | `general-biomedical-assistant` | Skill used when no match exceeds threshold |
| `workflow.step_timeout_seconds` | `120` | Timeout per workflow step |
| `workflow.retry_count` | `2` | Retries on step failure with exponential backoff |
| `system.enable_safety_checks` | `true` | Enables clinical safety scanning on output |
| `system.log_json` | `false` | Structured JSON logging to stderr |

Sources: [config.yaml](biokernel/config.yaml#L1-L76), [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L153-L156)

## Running the MCP Server

The server is launched as a standalone Python process. An MCP client (like Claude Desktop) configures it as a command in its MCP settings:

```bash
# Direct execution
python -m biokernel.biokernel.mcp_server

# Or via the entry point
python biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py
```

On startup, the server initializes the BioKernel (which discovers skills, builds the routing index, and connects LLM providers), logs the number of loaded skills to stderr, and begins reading JSON-RPC messages from stdin. The client then performs the MCP handshake and can begin calling tools.

Sources: [mcp_server.py](biokernel/biokernel/mcp_server.py#L385-L391)

## What Comes Next

The MCP Protocol Server is the external interface of a deeper orchestration stack. To understand how skill routing works under the hood, see [Semantic Skill Router](5-semantic-skill-router). To understand how multi-step workflows are parallelized and retried, see [DAG Workflow Engine](6-dag-workflow-engine). To understand how the same BioKernel capabilities are exposed via REST API (as opposed to MCP), see [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview). To explore how LLM providers are abstracted behind a unified interface, see [LLM Provider Adapters](9-llm-provider-adapters).

# USDL Transpiler



The **USDL Transpiler** is the compile-time bridge between declarative skill definitions and executable LLM prompts. It transforms a single, model-agnostic **Universal Skill Description Language (USDL)** specification into provider-optimized artifacts for Anthropic, OpenAI, and Gemini — eliminating the need to author and maintain separate prompt files for each LLM backend. Write a skill once in USDL; the transpiler emits the system prompts, function schemas, XML structures, and safety guardrails that each provider expects natively.

Sources: [usdl_transpiler.py](biokernel/optimizer/usdl_transpiler.py#L1-L22), [USDL_OVERVIEW.md](docs/USDL_OVERVIEW.md#L17-L28)

## Why a Transpiler?

Biomedical AI skills are complex: they carry input/output contracts, safety policies, audit requirements, and domain-specific instructions. Maintaining these across three fundamentally different LLM APIs is error-prone and leads to **drift** — the OpenAI version of a clinical skill subtly diverges from the Anthropic version, creating compliance risk. The transpiler enforces a **single source of truth**: the USDL spec. Every compiled artifact is derived, never hand-authored, so safety checks and audit policies travel identically to every provider.

| Pain Point | Without Transpiler | With Transpiler |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt format | Hand-write XML for Claude, JSON Schema for OpenAI, role cards for Gemini | Auto-generated from one spec |
| Safety policy sync | Copy-paste across providers; drift inevitable | Compiled into every artifact automatically |
| Tool schema format | `input_schema` for Claude, `parameters` for OpenAI, text descriptions for Gemini | Schema helpers emit correct dialect per provider |
| Adding a new skill | Write 3+ prompt variants | Write 1 USDL JSON; call `compile_all()` |
| Audit traceability | Manual | `audit_policy` embedded in every payload |

Sources: [USDL_OVERVIEW.md](docs/USDL_OVERVIEW.md#L35-L44), [usdl_transpiler.py](biokernel/optimizer/usdl_transpiler.py#L96-L116)

## Architecture: From Spec to Provider Artifact

The transpiler sits between the **USDL schema layer** and the **LLM provider adapter layer**. It consumes a `USDLSpec` (the canonical intermediate representation) and emits a dictionary of provider-specific payloads. The adapters then consume these payloads at runtime through the `LLMProvider` interface.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Sources
        A["USDL JSON<br/>(usdl_schema_v1.json)"]
        B["SKILL.md<br/>(YAML frontmatter)"]
        C["YAML File"]
    end

    subgraph "USDL Transpiler Core"
        D["USDLSpec<br/>(Intermediate Representation)"]
        E["_compile_openai()"]
        F["_compile_anthropic()"]
        G["_compile_gemini()"]
    end

    subgraph "Provider Artifacts"
        H["system_message +<br/>function_schemas +<br/>output_schema"]
        I["system_prompt (XML) +<br/>tool_definitions"]
        J["prompt (role card) +<br/>output_constraints"]
    end

    A -->|from_dict| D
    B -->|from_skill_md| D
    C -->|from_yaml_file| D
    D --> E
    D --> F
    D --> G
    E --> H
    F --> I
    G --> J
```

Sources: [usdl_transpiler.py](biokernel/optimizer/usdl_transpiler.py#L34-L93), [usdl_schema_v1.json](biokernel/schema/usdl_schema_v1.json#L1-L30)

## The USDLSpec Intermediate Representation

The `USDLSpec` dataclass is the transpiler's internal model — a normalized view of a biomedical skill that strips away format-specific noise (JSON vs YAML vs Markdown) and exposes only what the compilation passes need. Three factory methods parse different source formats into this same representation:

| Factory Method | Source Format | Key Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `USDLSpec.from_dict()` | Parsed JSON/YAML dict | Direct field mapping; no inference |
| `USDLSpec.from_skill_md()` | SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter | Parses `---`-delimited frontmatter via PyYAML; infers safety checks by scanning body for keywords like "safety", "risk", "contraindication" |
| `USDLSpec.from_yaml_file()` | Standalone YAML file | Loads via `yaml.safe_load()`, unwraps `skill:` key if present, delegates to `from_dict()` |

The dataclass fields map directly to the transpilation concerns:

- **`name` / `description`** — Used in system prompt headers across all providers
- **`inputs` / `outputs`** — Lists of `FieldSpec` objects; compiled into JSON Schema (OpenAI), XML field definitions (Anthropic), or plain-text input/output blocks (Gemini)
- **`safety_checks`** — String list injected verbatim into every provider's output; never omitted
- **`audit_policy`** — Defaults to "Log decisions to event bus"; embedded in every compiled artifact
- **`instructions_body`** — The freeform instruction text that forms the core of the system prompt
- **`version` / `category`** — Metadata carried through for observability

Sources: [usdl_transpiler.py](biokernel/optimizer/usdl_transpiler.py#L34-L93), [USDL_SPEC_PRIOR_AUTH.json](Skills/USDL_SPEC_PRIOR_AUTH.json#L1-L40)

## Provider-Specific Compilation

The `USDLTranspiler.compile()` method dispatches to one of three private compilation methods based on the `Provider` enum. Each method produces a distinct artifact structure optimized for its target LLM's native strengths.

### OpenAI Compilation

The OpenAI path produces a **system message + function schemas + output schema** bundle. The system message is a Markdown-structured string combining the skill description, instructions body, and safety checks. Function schemas follow the OpenAI function calling format using the `parameters` key (not `input_schema`). The output schema is a standard JSON Schema object with `properties` and `required` arrays.

```python
# Result structure from _compile_openai()
{
    "provider": "openai",
    "system_message": "You are the 'Prior Authorization Agent' biomedical agent. ...",
    "function_schemas": [{
        "name": "prior_authorization_agent",
        "description": "Review prior authorization requests...",
        "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {...}, "required": [...]}
    }],
    "output_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {...}, "required": [...]},
    "safety_checks": ["Never hallucinate policy references.", ...],
    "audit_policy": "Post determination + trace to event bus..."
}
```

### Anthropic Compilation

The Anthropic path renders a **fully XML-structured system prompt** that leverages Claude's strength at parsing tagged content. The `_render_xml_prompt()` method wraps every element — role, description, version, instructions, inputs, outputs, safety, audit — in semantic XML tags. Tool definitions use the `input_schema` key (matching Claude's API contract, distinct from OpenAI's `parameters`).

```xml
<system>
  <role>Prior Authorization Agent</role>
  <description>Review prior authorization requests...</description>
  <version>1.0.0</version>
  <instructions>...</instructions>
  <inputs>
    <input name='clinical_note' type='string' required='True'>...</input>
    <input name='procedure_code' type='string' required='True'>...</input>
  </inputs>
  <outputs>
    <output name='decision' type='string'>APPROVED or DENIED</output>
    <output name='rationale' type='string'>Clinical reasoning</output>
  </outputs>
  <safety>
    <policy>Never hallucinate policy references.</policy>
    <policy>Escalate unclear cases to human reviewers.</policy>
  </safety>
  <audit>Post determination + trace to event bus...</audit>
</system>
```

### Gemini Compilation

The Gemini path generates a **plain-text role card** with clear section separators — a format that plays to Gemini's strength at long-context reasoning and structured input parsing. Inputs and outputs are rendered as bulleted lists with type annotations. Safety checks are listed under a dedicated "Safety:" section.

```python
# Result structure from _compile_gemini()
{
    "provider": "gemini",
    "prompt": "Role: Prior Authorization Agent\nObjective: ...\n--- INSTRUCTIONS ---\n...\n---\nInputs:\n- clinical_note (string): ...\nExpected Outputs:\n- decision (string): ...\nSafety:\n- Never hallucinate policy references.",
    "output_constraints": ["decision", "rationale"],
    "audit_policy": "..."
}
```

Sources: [usdl_transpiler.py](biokernel/optimizer/usdl_transpiler.py#L127-L248), [USDL_OVERVIEW.md](docs/USDL_OVERVIEW.md#L20-L27)

## Schema Helpers and Key Differences

The transpiler's private schema helpers translate `FieldSpec` lists into the dialect each provider expects. The difference is subtle but critical: **OpenAI uses `parameters` while Anthropic uses `input_schema`** — both containing the same JSON Schema structure underneath.

| Aspect | OpenAI | Anthropic | Gemini |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tool schema key | `parameters` | `input_schema` | Not used (text-based) |
| Prompt structure | Markdown system message | XML-tagged system prompt | Plain-text role card |
| Output definition | `output_schema` (JSON Schema) | XML `<outputs>` tags | `output_constraints` (name list) |
| Safety injection | Appended to system message as `### Safety` section | Wrapped in `<safety><policy>` tags | Bulleted `Safety:` section |
| Thinking support | Not included (add via meta-prompter) | XML structure supports `<thinking>` blocks | "Think step-by-step" hint |

> [!TIP]
> The `_openai_functions()` and `_anthropic_tools()` methods produce nearly identical JSON Schema objects internally — the only difference is the top-level key name (`parameters` vs `input_schema`). If you extend the transpiler for a new provider, reuse `_json_schema()` for the schema body and only change the wrapper key.

Sources: [usdl_transpiler.py](biokernel/optimizer/usdl_transpiler.py#L218-L248), [anthropic_adapter.py](biokernel/adapters/anthropic_adapter.py#L274-L280)

## Compilation Workflow: End to End

The following diagram traces the full path from a USDL JSON source file through transpilation to runtime execution via the adapter layer:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["Skills/USDL_SPEC_PRIOR_AUTH.json"] -->|"json.load()"| B["USDLSpec.from_dict()"]
    B --> C["USDLSpec IR"]
    C --> D["USDLTranspiler.compile()"]
    D --> E["_compile_openai()"]
    D --> F["_compile_anthropic()"]
    D --> G["_compile_gemini()"]

    E --> H["OpenAI Artifact"]
    F --> I["Anthropic Artifact"]
    G --> J["Gemini Artifact"]

    H --> K["LLMFactory.create_provider('openai', config)"]
    I --> L["LLMFactory.create_provider('anthropic', config)"]
    J --> M["LLMFactory.create_provider('gemini', config)"]

    K --> N["OpenAIRuntimeAdapter.generate()"]
    L --> O["AnthropicAdapter.generate()"]
    M --> P["GeminiAdapter.generate()"]

    N --> Q["LLMResponse"]
    O --> Q
    P --> Q
```

Sources: [usdl_transpiler.py](biokernel/optimizer/usdl_transpiler.py#L96-L116), [factory.py](biokernel/adapters/factory.py#L61-L97), [USDL_OVERVIEW.md](docs/USDL_OVERVIEW.md#L30-L42)

## Using the Transpiler

### Programmatic API

The primary interface is `USDLTranspiler.compile(spec, provider)`, which returns a `Dict[str, Any]` containing the provider-specific artifact. Use `compile_all()` to generate artifacts for every provider simultaneously.

```python
from biokernel.optimizer.usdl_transpiler import USDLTranspiler, USDLSpec, Provider
import json

# Load from a USDL JSON file
spec = USDLSpec.from_dict(json.load(open("Skills/USDL_SPEC_PRIOR_AUTH.json")))

# Compile for a single provider
transpiler = USDLTranspiler()
openai_payload = transpiler.compile(spec, Provider.OPENAI)
anthropic_payload = transpiler.compile(spec, Provider.ANTHROPIC)
gemini_payload = transpiler.compile(spec, Provider.GEMINI)

# Compile for all providers at once
all_artifacts = transpiler.compile_all(spec)
# Returns: {"openai": {...}, "anthropic": {...}, "gemini": {...}}
```

### Loading from SKILL.md

The `from_skill_md()` class method parses Markdown files with YAML frontmatter — the standard skill authoring format in this platform. It extracts `name` and `description` from the frontmatter and treats the remaining body as `instructions_body`. Safety checks are inferred automatically by scanning the body for safety-critical keywords.

```python
with open("Skills/Genomics/single_cell_qc/SKILL.md") as f:
    spec = USDLSpec.from_skill_md(f.read())

artifact = transpiler.compile(spec, Provider.ANTHROPIC)
```

### CLI Usage

The transpiler includes a built-in CLI for quick artifact inspection. Pass `--file` with a YAML/JSON path and an optional provider name:

```bash
# Default: runs a demo with the built-in Prior Auth spec
python -m biokernel.optimizer.usdl_transpiler

# Compile a specific file for Anthropic
python -m biokernel.optimizer.usdl_transpiler --file Skills/USDL_SPEC_PRIOR_AUTH.json anthropic

# Compile for OpenAI
python -m biokernel.optimizer.usdl_transpiler --file my_skill.yaml openai
```

Sources: [usdl_transpiler.py](biokernel/optimizer/usdl_transpiler.py#L278-L326), [USDL_OVERVIEW.md](docs/USDL_OVERVIEW.md#L30-L42), [TUTORIAL_USDL_TRANSPILER.md](biokernel/optimizer/TUTORIAL_USDL_TRANSPILER.md#L28-L62)

## The Prompt Optimizer Companion

Alongside the structural transpiler, the `meta_prompter.py` module provides **runtime prompt optimization** — applying provider-specific prompt engineering best practices to any biomedical query. While the transpiler compiles *skill structure* (inputs, outputs, schemas), the meta-prompter optimizes *prompt content* (formatting, thinking cues, safety framing).

| Optimization Target | Claude Strategy | OpenAI Strategy | Gemini Strategy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Structure | XML tags (`<system>`, `<instructions>`, `<user_query>`) | Markdown sections (`### SYSTEM`, `### USER`) | Role card + separator lines (`====`) |
| Reasoning | "Think step-by-step" + XML framing | Concise system instruction + format hints | "Provide comprehensive, multi-faceted analysis" |
| Safety | `<safety_guidelines>` XML block | Inline `SAFETY:` block | Bulleted `Safety Requirements:` section |
| Evidence | "Cite sources with PMIDs or DOIs" | "Cite sources when possible" | "Include citations to primary literature" |

> [!TIP]
> The transpiler and meta-prompter operate at different layers and compose cleanly. Use the transpiler to build the *skill skeleton* (system prompt + schemas), then pass the user's actual query through the meta-prompter before sending it to the adapter. This separation ensures structural consistency (transpiler) and content optimization (meta-prompter) evolve independently.

Sources: [meta_prompter.py](biokernel/optimizer/meta_prompter.py#L1-L34), [meta_prompter.py](biokernel/optimizer/meta_prompter.py#L62-L165)

## USDL Schema v1: The Contract

The canonical JSON Schema at [usdl_schema_v1.json](biokernel/schema/usdl_schema_v1.json) defines the full contract for USDL specifications. Beyond the core fields that the transpiler consumes, the schema includes several forward-looking sections that future optimizer passes will leverage:

| Schema Section | Purpose | Transpiler Status |
|---|---|---|
| `skill.id` | Unique identifier in `domain.category.name` format | Carried as metadata |
| `skill.capabilities` | Named capability entries with inputs/outputs | Mapped to `FieldSpec` lists |
| `skill.prompts` | System prompt, user template, few-shot examples | Mapped to `instructions_body` |
| `skill.tools` | Python functions, API endpoints, MCP tools, shell commands | Not yet compiled (reserved for DAG engine) |
| `skill.dependencies` | Python packages, system deps, data, models | Not yet compiled (reserved for runtime) |
| `skill.platform_configs` | Per-provider flags (MCP server, GPT actions, Gemini extension) | Partially used via `compile()` |
| `skill.validation.test_cases` | Input/output assertion pairs | Not yet compiled (reserved for evaluator) |
| `skill.evals` | Automated eval cases with assertions (contains, regex, biomedical_entity) | Not yet compiled (reserved for evaluation framework) |
| `skill.optimization` | Target metrics and platform-specific hints | Partially used via meta-prompter |

Sources: [usdl_schema_v1.json](biokernel/schema/usdl_schema_v1.json#L1-L200), [usdl_schema_v1.json](biokernel/schema/usdl_schema_v1.json#L200-L318)

## Real-World Example: Prior Authorization Coworker

The repository includes a production-grade USDL spec at `Skills/USDL_SPEC_PRIOR_AUTH.json` — a **Prior Authorization Coworker** that evaluates medical necessity requests against payer policy. This spec demonstrates all transpiler features:

- **Two inputs**: `clinical_note` (unstructured text) and `procedure_code` (CPT/HCPCS code)
- **Three outputs**: `decision` (APPROVED/DENIED), `justification` (policy criteria array), `escalation_required` (boolean)
- **Three safety checks**: Quote payer policy verbatim, escalate on incomplete data, never invent patient data
- **Explicit audit policy**: Persist every response plus thinking trace to BioKernel AuditLog

When compiled through the transpiler, this single 40-line JSON produces three complete provider artifacts — each with the correct schema dialect, prompt structure, and embedded safety policies — ready for immediate use with the adapter layer.

Sources: [USDL_SPEC_PRIOR_AUTH.json](Skills/USDL_SPEC_PRIOR_AUTH.json#L1-L40), [usdl_transpiler.py](biokernel/optimizer/usdl_transpiler.py#L278-L314)

## What Comes Next

The transpiler is the first stage in the cross-provider pipeline. After compilation, the generated artifacts flow into the adapter layer for actual LLM invocation:

- **[LLM Provider Adapters](9-llm-provider-adapters)** — How each adapter (`AnthropicAdapter`, `OpenAIRuntimeAdapter`, `GeminiAdapter`) consumes transpiler output and translates it into provider API calls, including multi-turn agentic loops with tool execution
- **[Semantic Skill Router](5-semantic-skill-router)** — How incoming queries are matched to USDL specs before transpilation occurs
- **[DAG Workflow Engine](6-dag-workflow-engine)** — How the `skill.tools` definitions in USDL specs will be compiled into executable workflow graphs
- **[Biomedical Evaluation Framework](13-biomedical-evaluation-framework)** — How the `skill.evals` section enables automated testing of compiled skills across providers

# LLM Provider Adapters



BioKernel's adapter layer is the **bridge between provider-agnostic skill logic and provider-specific API realities**. It exists in two distinct layers: a *Runtime Adapter Layer* that normalizes LLM inference calls into a unified `LLMRequest`/`LLMResponse` contract, and a *USDL Platform Adapter Layer* that transpiles skill definitions into provider-native deployment formats (Custom GPTs, MCP Servers, Assistants, OpenAPI specs). This dual-layer architecture is what makes the "write once, run on any provider" promise real — skills express intent once in USDL, and adapters handle both execution-time translation and deployment-time packaging.

Sources: [factory.py](/biokernel/adapters/factory.py#L1-L119), [llm_provider.py](/biokernel/interface/llm_provider.py#L1-L121), [claude_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/claude_adapter.py#L1-L50), [openai_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/openai_adapter.py#L1-L50)

## Architectural Overview

The adapter system follows a **Strategy + Factory + Registry** pattern. The `LLMProvider` abstract base class defines the contract; concrete adapters implement provider-specific translation; the `LLMFactory` manages registration, instantiation, and caching. Separately, the USDL adapters (`ClaudeAdapter`, `OpenAIAdapter`) operate at the skill-definition level, converting declarative USDL YAML into provider-native artifacts.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "BioKernel Orchestration"
        A[Skill Router] --> B[AgentRequest]
        B --> C[LLMFactory]
    end

    subgraph "Runtime Adapter Layer"
        C -->|create_provider| D[AnthropicAdapter]
        C -->|create_provider| E[OpenAIRuntimeAdapter]
        C -->|create_provider| F[GeminiAdapter]
        C -->|create_provider| G[LocalAdapter]
        D & E & F & G -->|normalize| H[LLMResponse]
    end

    subgraph "USDL Platform Adapter Layer"
        I[USDL YAML] --> J[ClaudeAdapter]
        I --> K[OpenAIAdapter]
        J --> L[MCP Server Config + SKILL.md + tool_use Schema]
        K --> M[Custom GPT + Assistant + Function Schemas + OpenAPI Spec]
    end

    subgraph "Unified Schema"
        N[LLMRequest] --> D & E & F & G
        H --> O[AgentResponse]
    end

    style C fill:#2563eb,color:#fff
    style H fill:#16a34a,color:#fff
    style I fill:#9333ea,color:#fff
```

> [!TIP]
> The Runtime Adapter Layer and USDL Platform Adapter Layer serve fundamentally different lifecycle stages: runtime adapters are invoked per-request during skill execution, while USDL adapters run once during skill packaging/deployment. Don't confuse `AnthropicAdapter` (runtime inference) with `ClaudeAdapter` (USDL-to-Claude format transpilation).

Sources: [factory.py](/biokernel/adapters/factory.py#L30-L60), [runtime_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/runtime_adapter.py#L1-L92), [claude_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/claude_adapter.py#L24-L48), [openai_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/openai_adapter.py#L25-L51)

## The LLMProvider Contract

Every runtime adapter must implement the `LLMProvider` abstract base class. This contract is the **single source of truth** for what "being a provider" means inside BioKernel. It defines five core operations plus two convenience methods:

| Method | Purpose | Return Type |
|---|---|---|
| `initialize(config)` | Configure API keys, model selection, and validate connectivity | `bool` |
| `provider_name` | Canonical provider identifier (e.g., `"anthropic"`, `"openai"`) | `str` |
| `is_available` | Runtime health flag — `True` only after successful initialization | `bool` |
| `generate(request)` | Single-turn LLM inference with full schema normalization | `LLMResponse` |
| `generate_with_tools(request, tool_executor, max_iterations)` | Multi-turn agentic loop: generate → tool_call → execute → feed back | `LLMResponse` |
| `stream(request)` | Token-by-token streaming (falls back to `generate()` if unsupported) | `AsyncIterator[str]` |
| `check_health()` | Probe provider reachability and latency | `Dict[str, Any]` |

The contract enforces that all input and output flows through the unified `LLMRequest` and `LLMResponse` Pydantic models, meaning the orchestration layer never sees raw provider APIs — only the normalized schema.

Sources: [llm_provider.py](/biokernel/interface/llm_provider.py#L30-L121)

## Unified I/O Schema

The `LLMRequest` and `LLMResponse` models are the **interchange format** that makes provider switching transparent. Every adapter translates between its native API and these schemas.

**LLMRequest** carries the full specification of what the orchestration layer needs:

| Field | Type | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `query` | `str` | *(required)* | Primary user prompt |
| `system_instruction` | `Optional[str]` | `None` | System-level directive |
| `messages` | `List[LLMMessage]` | `[]` | Multi-turn conversation history |
| `tools` | `Optional[List[ToolDefinition]]` | `None` | Available tools for function calling |
| `temperature` | `float` | `0.7` | Sampling randomness |
| `max_tokens` | `int` | `4096` | Maximum output length |
| `top_p` | `float` | `1.0` | Nucleus sampling threshold |
| `stop_sequences` | `Optional[List[str]]` | `None` | Custom stop triggers |
| `response_format` | `Optional[str]` | `None` | `"json"` for structured output |
| `stream` | `bool` | `False` | Enable streaming mode |
| `context` | `Dict[str, Any]` | `{}` | Arbitrary execution context |

**LLMResponse** normalizes what comes back, regardless of provider:

| Field | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | `str` | Generated text content |
| `tool_calls` | `Optional[List[ToolCall]]` | Tool invocations requested by the model |
| `finish_reason` | `FinishReason` | `STOP`, `LENGTH`, `TOOL_CALLS`, `CONTENT_FILTER`, `ERROR` |
| `usage` | `Dict[str, int]` | Token counts: `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, `total_tokens` |
| `latency_ms` | `float` | End-to-end latency measurement |
| `provider` | `str` | Which adapter served this response |
| `model` | `str` | Actual model identifier used |

Sources: [io_types.py](/biokernel/schema/io_types.py#L1-L130)

## LLMFactory: The Registry and Object Pool

The `LLMFactory` implements a **class-level registry** with lazy default registration and instance caching. It is the single entry point for the orchestration layer to obtain provider instances without coupling to concrete classes.

The factory's lifecycle works in three phases. **Registration** populates the `_registry` dict mapping canonical names to adapter classes — `register_defaults()` auto-registers the four built-in adapters (`anthropic`, `openai`, `gemini`, `local`), and `register_provider()` allows plugins to add custom adapters at runtime. **Creation** instantiates a provider, calls its `initialize()` method with provider-specific config, and optionally caches the instance for reuse. **Lookup** via `get_provider()` retrieves cached instances, while `list_providers()` reports availability status across all registered adapters.

```python
# Creating a provider through the factory
from biokernel.adapters.factory import LLMFactory

provider = LLMFactory.create_provider(
    "anthropic",
    {"api_key": "sk-ant-...", "model": "claude-sonnet-4-20250514"},
    cache=True
)

# Checking all registered providers
availability = LLMFactory.list_providers()
# {"anthropic": True, "openai": False, "gemini": False, "local": True}
```

> [!TIP]
> The `cache=True` default means calling `create_provider("anthropic", config)` twice returns the *same instance*. If you need a fresh provider (e.g., with different API keys for multi-tenant scenarios), pass `cache=False` or call `LLMFactory.reset()` to clear the pool.

Sources: [factory.py](/biokernel/adapters/factory.py#L30-L119)

## Runtime Adapter Deep Dive

### AnthropicAdapter

The `AnthropicAdapter` wraps the official `anthropic` Python SDK and provides **full-fidelity integration** with the Anthropic Messages API. It is the most feature-complete adapter in the system, supporting single-turn generation, multi-turn agentic tool-use loops, streaming, and the Claude-native content block model.

**Key translation patterns:**

| BioKernel Concept | Anthropic API Mapping |
|---|---|
| `LLMRequest.system_instruction` | `system` parameter (top-level, not in messages) |
| `ToolDefinition` | `{"name", "description", "input_schema"}` (Claude native format) |
| `ToolCall` | `content` block with `type: "tool_use"` |
| `ToolResult` | `{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id", "content"}` as user message |
| `FinishReason.STOP` | `stop_reason: "end_turn"` or `"stop_sequence"` |
| `FinishReason.TOOL_CALLS` | `stop_reason: "tool_use"` |

The `generate_with_tools()` method implements a full agentic loop: it sends the initial request, checks for `tool_use` content blocks, invokes the `tool_executor` for each, appends tool results as a user message, and loops until the model returns `end_turn` or the iteration limit is reached. The default model is `claude-sonnet-4-20250514`.

Sources: [anthropic_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/anthropic_adapter.py#L1-L297)

### OpenAIRuntimeAdapter

The `OpenAIRuntimeAdapter` wraps the `openai` Python SDK and targets the **Chat Completions API** with function calling. It supports JSON mode via `response_format`, translates tool definitions into OpenAI's function-calling envelope (`{"type": "function", "function": {...}}`), and handles the assistant/tool message flow required by the OpenAI conversation format.

**Key translation patterns:**

| BioKernel Concept | OpenAI API Mapping |
|---|---|
| `LLMRequest.system_instruction` | `{"role": "system", "content": ...}` as first message |
| `ToolDefinition` | `{"type": "function", "function": {"name", "description", "parameters"}}` |
| `ToolCall` | `choice.message.tool_calls[i].function` (JSON-parsed arguments) |
| `ToolResult` | `{"role": "tool", "tool_call_id", "content"}` message |
| `response_format="json"` | `response_format={"type": "json_object"}` |
| `FinishReason.STOP` | `finish_reason: "stop"` |

The agentic loop follows the same generate→tool_call→execute→feed-back pattern as the Anthropic adapter, but uses OpenAI's message format where the assistant message (including tool calls) is appended as-is via `model_dump()`, and tool results are appended as role=`tool` messages. The default model is `gpt-4o`.

Sources: [openai_runtime_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/openai_runtime_adapter.py#L1-L274)

### GeminiAdapter

The `GeminiAdapter` wraps the `google-generativeai` SDK and targets the **Gemini GenerativeModel API**. It supports single-turn generation with system instructions and a prompt-based approach to tool use. Because the Gemini SDK's native function calling API differs significantly from the agentic loop pattern, the adapter embeds tool descriptions directly into the prompt with structured output instructions (`TOOL_CALL: <name>(<args>)` and `FINAL_ANSWER: <answer>` markers).

**Key characteristics:**

- Default model: `gemini-2.0-flash`
- System instructions are applied by creating a new `GenerativeModel` instance with the `system_instruction` parameter
- Token usage is estimated via character-count heuristic (`len(text) // 4`) rather than exact API reporting
- The `generate_with_tools()` method delegates to `generate()` with an enhanced prompt — it does not perform a true multi-turn agentic loop

Sources: [gemini_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/gemini_adapter.py#L1-L165)

### LocalAdapter

The `LocalAdapter` provides connectivity to **self-hosted models** through two backends: Ollama (preferred, via the `ollama` Python SDK) and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (vLLM, llama.cpp server, LM Studio) via `httpx`. Initialization probes connectivity by trying Ollama first (`ollama.list()`), then falling back to an HTTP GET to `{api_base}/api/tags`.

**Backend comparison:**

| Aspect | Ollama Backend | OpenAI-Compatible Backend |
|---|---|---|
| Connection test | `ollama.list()` | `GET {api_base}/api/tags` |
| Request format | `ollama.chat(model, messages, options)` | `POST {api_base}/v1/chat/completions` |
| Token reporting | `prompt_eval_count` + `eval_count` from response | `usage` from JSON response |
| Default model | `llama3.1:8b` | `llama3.1:8b` |
| Default base URL | `http://localhost:11434` | `http://localhost:11434` |

Tool use follows the same prompt-embedding strategy as the Gemini adapter — tool descriptions are injected into the query text since most local models have limited native function-calling support.

Sources: [local_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/local_adapter.py#L1-L206)

## RuntimeLLMAdapter: The Convenience Singleton

The `RuntimeLLMAdapter` provides a **backward-compatible synchronous interface** for code that expects a simple `complete(system, user_prompt, model)` call rather than the async `generate()` API. It acts as a facade over the factory, automatically selecting the best available provider in preference order: `anthropic → openai → gemini → local`.

The preference cascade reads API keys from environment variables (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY`) and initializes the first provider that reports `is_available == True`. A module-level singleton `llm = RuntimeLLMAdapter()` is exported for legacy imports. When called from an already-running event loop, it offloads to a `ThreadPoolExecutor` to avoid blocking.

```python
# Legacy synchronous usage
from biokernel.adapters.runtime_adapter import llm

result = llm.complete(
    system="You are a biomedical assistant.",
    user_prompt="Explain BRCA1 pathogenic variants."
)
```

Sources: [runtime_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/runtime_adapter.py#L1-L92)

## USDL Platform Adapters

While runtime adapters handle *inference*, the USDL platform adapters handle *deployment packaging*. They take a declarative USDL YAML skill definition and produce provider-native deployment artifacts.

### ClaudeAdapter (USDL → Claude)

The `ClaudeAdapter` converts USDL skill definitions into three Claude-specific formats plus a hooks configuration:

| Output Artifact | Format | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **SKILL.md** | Markdown | Claude Code skill definition with capabilities, inputs/outputs, system prompts, and examples |
| **MCP Server Config** | JSON | Model Context Protocol server with tools, resources, and prompts for Claude integration |
| **tool_use Schema** | JSON | Claude API `tool_use` format with `name`, `description`, and `input_schema` per capability |
| **Hooks Config** | JSON | Claude Code hooks for pre/post execution validation |

The adapter maps USDL types to JSON Schema types (e.g., `AnnData → string` representing a file path, `DataFrame → string` representing a JSON string), and converts each USDL capability into a Claude tool definition. The MCP server config includes a system prompt resource that can be loaded at runtime.

Sources: [claude_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/claude_adapter.py#L24-L327)

### OpenAIAdapter (USDL → OpenAI)

The `OpenAIAdapter` converts USDL skill definitions into four OpenAI-specific formats:

| Output Artifact | Format | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Custom GPT Config** | JSON | GPT Builder configuration with instructions, conversation starters, and capabilities |
| **Assistant Config** | JSON | Assistants API format with tools (code_interpreter + function tools), instructions, and metadata |
| **Function Schemas** | JSON | Function calling definitions compatible with `tools` parameter |
| **OpenAPI Spec** | YAML | OpenAPI 3.0 specification for GPT Actions with security schemes |

The OpenAI adapter adds intelligent defaults: it enables `code_interpreter` when Python dependencies exist in the skill, generates conversation starters from prompt examples (falling back to generic biomedical prompts), and maps each capability to both a function schema and an OpenAPI POST endpoint. The OpenAPI spec includes `ApiKeyAuth` security by default.

Sources: [openai_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/openai_adapter.py#L25-L368)

## Adapter Capability Matrix

The following table summarizes feature support across all four runtime adapters:

| Feature | Anthropic | OpenAI | Gemini | Local |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Single-turn generation | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Multi-turn agentic loop | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠ Prompt-based | ⚠ Prompt-based |
| Native tool/function calling | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Streaming | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| JSON mode | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| System instruction | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Exact token usage | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ Estimated | ✅ (Ollama) |
| Health check | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Async client | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (httpx) |
| Default model | claude-sonnet-4 | gpt-4o | gemini-2.0-flash | llama3.1:8b |

Sources: [anthropic_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/anthropic_adapter.py#L38-L55), [openai_runtime_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/openai_runtime_adapter.py#L33-L50), [gemini_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/gemini_adapter.py#L30-L46), [local_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/local_adapter.py#L32-L49)

## Configuration Reference

Provider behavior is configured through `biokernel/config.yaml` and environment variables. The factory reads this config at initialization time to set model names, API key sources, and default parameters.

```yaml
# biokernel/config.yaml
default_provider: "anthropic"  # anthropic | openai | gemini | local

providers:
  anthropic:
    model: "claude-sonnet-4-20250514"
    api_key_env: "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
    max_tokens: 4096
    temperature: 0.3

  openai:
    model: "gpt-4o"
    api_key_env: "OPENAI_API_KEY"
    max_tokens: 4096
    temperature: 0.3

  gemini:
    model: "gemini-2.0-flash"
    api_key_env: "GOOGLE_API_KEY"
    max_tokens: 4096
    temperature: 0.3

  local:
    model: "llama3.1:8b"
    api_base: "http://localhost:11434"
    max_tokens: 4096
    temperature: 0.3
```

Each adapter's `initialize()` method resolves the API key by checking `config.get("api_key")` first, then falling back to `os.getenv(config.get("api_key_env"))`. This two-tier resolution supports both direct key injection (for testing) and environment-variable-based configuration (for production).

Sources: [config.yaml](/biokernel/config.yaml#L1-L76), [anthropic_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/anthropic_adapter.py#L65-L83), [openai_runtime_adapter.py](/biokernel/adapters/openai_runtime_adapter.py#L52-L70)

## Extending with Custom Providers

The factory's `register_provider()` class method enables **runtime plugin registration** without modifying core code. Any class that implements the `LLMProvider` interface can be registered:

```python
from biokernel.adapters.factory import LLMFactory
from biokernel.interface.llm_provider import LLMProvider

class MyCustomProvider(LLMProvider):
    @property
    def provider_name(self) -> str:
        return "custom"

    @property
    def is_available(self) -> bool:
        return self._available

    def initialize(self, config):
        # Your setup logic
        self._available = True
        return True

    async def generate(self, request):
        # Your inference logic, returning LLMResponse
        ...

    async def generate_with_tools(self, request, tool_executor=None, max_iterations=10):
        # Your agentic loop logic, returning LLMResponse
        ...

# Register before any create_provider() call
LLMFactory.register_provider("custom", MyCustomProvider)
```

After registration, the custom provider is available through the same `LLMFactory.create_provider("custom", config)` interface used by all built-in adapters, and will appear in `LLMFactory.list_providers()` output.

Sources: [factory.py](/biokernel/adapters/factory.py#L38-L47), [llm_provider.py](/biokernel/interface/llm_provider.py#L30-L121)

## Provider Skill Coverage

Beyond the runtime adapters, BioKernel maintains curated operational skills for each provider under `Skills/AI_Providers/`. These skills capture provider-specific operational knowledge — SDK migration paths, deprecation timelines, rate-limit behavior, and cloud deployment tradeoffs:

| Skill Directory | Provider Focus |
|---|---|
| `OpenAI_Platform_Operations_2026/` | Responses API, model selection, migration workflows |
| `Anthropic_Claude_Operations_2026/` | Claude API, deprecation notes, tool-use patterns |
| `Google_Gemini_Operations_2026/` | Gemini model and GenAI SDK operations |
| `AWS_Bedrock_Operations_2026/` | Bedrock Converse API, Guardrails, AgentCore |
| `Azure_AI_Foundry_Operations_2026/` | Azure AI Foundry deployments, identity, safety |
| `Cohere_Platform_Operations_2026/` | Cohere rerank/embed/transcribe surfaces |
| `DeepSeek_API_Operations_2026/` | DeepSeek model integration |
| `Mistral_Platform_Operations_2026/` | Mistral platform operations |
| `XAI_Grok_Operations_2026/` | xAI Grok integration |
| `Frontier_OSS_Models_2026/` | Open-source model ecosystems and deployment |
| `Cloud_AI_Operations_AWS_Azure_2026/` | Cross-cloud deployment tradeoffs |

These skills are distinct from the runtime adapters — they provide **operational guidance** for developers working with specific provider APIs, while the adapters provide **programmatic abstraction** for the BioKernel engine.

Sources: [README.md](/Skills/AI_Providers/README.md#L1-L50)

## Navigation

The adapter layer sits between the [USDL Transpiler](8-usdl-transpiler) (which generates the USDL definitions that platform adapters consume) and the [Semantic Skill Router](5-semantic-skill-router) (which selects skills that runtime adapters execute). For configuration details of all provider settings, see [Configuration Reference](15-configuration-reference). To understand how tool-use flows through the agentic loop at the workflow level, see [DAG Workflow Engine](6-dag-workflow-engine).

# Genomics and Single-Cell Agents



The genomics and single-cell agent ecosystem represents the most expansive domain within the Universal Biomedical Skills platform, spanning over 50 individual skills and 12 specialized AI agents that collectively cover the entire continuum from raw sequencing reads to spatially resolved multi-omics tissue atlases. This domain is organized around two **orchestrators** — one for bulk genomics pipelines and one for single-cell workflows — that route natural language queries to the appropriate skill using keyword-weighted scoring and optional LLM-based semantic matching. The architecture follows a consistent pattern: each agent exposes a `SKILL.md` manifest declaring its capabilities, measurable outcomes, and guardrails; an orchestrator decomposes user intent into skill invocations; and the BioKernel's DAG engine executes the resulting workflow with traceability and safety checks.

## Architecture: Dual-Orchestrator Routing Model

The genomics and single-cell domain is governed by two independent but interoperable orchestrators. The **Genomics Orchestrator** manages bulk sequencing workflows — variant calling, alignment, VCF operations, CNV detection, and epigenomics — while the **Single-Cell Orchestrator** handles scRNA-seq preprocessing, batch integration, trajectory inference, cell communication, and multi-ome analysis. Both orchestrators share an identical routing architecture: a `KEYWORD_MAP` dictionary maps domain-specific terms to skill identifiers, a `route_query()` function scores candidate skills by cumulative keyword length, and a `route_query_with_mode()` function optionally delegates to an LLM-based router for semantic disambiguation. When no keywords match, the Genomics Orchestrator falls back to `genomics-qc` and the Single-Cell Orchestrator falls back to `sc-preprocessing`, ensuring every query produces a deterministic result.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph "User Query Layer"
        Q1["'Call variants from my BAM file'"]
        Q2["'Remove doublets and annotate cell types'"]
        Q3["'Identify spatial niches in tumor'"]
    end

    subgraph "Orchestrator Routing"
        direction TB
        GO["Genomics Orchestrator<br/>KEYWORD_MAP: 35+ entries<br/>10 skills"]
        SO["Single-Cell Orchestrator<br/>KEYWORD_MAP: 30+ entries<br/>9 skills"]
        RM{"Routing Mode"}
        KW["keyword — weighted score"]
        LLM["llm — semantic match"]
        HYB["hybrid — keyword → LLM fallback"]
    end

    subgraph "Genomics Skills"
        G1[genomics-variant-calling]
        G2[genomics-sv-detection]
        G3[genomics-vcf-operations]
        G4[genomics-alignment]
        G5[genomics-variant-annotation]
        G6[genomics-assembly]
        G7[genomics-phasing]
        G8[genomics-cnv-calling]
        G9[genomics-qc]
        G10[genomics-epigenomics]
    end

    subgraph "Single-Cell Skills"
        S1[sc-preprocessing]
        S2[sc-doublet-detection]
        S3[sc-cell-annotation]
        S4[sc-trajectory]
        S5[sc-batch-integration]
        S6[sc-de]
        S7[sc-grn]
        S8[sc-cell-communication]
        S9[sc-multiome]
    end

    Q1 --> GO
    Q2 --> SO
    Q3 --> SO

    GO --> RM
    SO --> RM
    RM --> KW & LLM & HYB

    KW --> G1 & G2 & G3 & G4 & G5 & G6 & G7 & G8 & G9 & G10
    KW --> S1 & S2 & S3 & S4 & S5 & S6 & S7 & S8 & S9
```

The routing algorithm uses **cumulative keyword length** as a scoring heuristic: for each keyword present in the lowercased query, the matched skill accumulates a score equal to the keyword's character length. The skill with the highest score wins, and confidence is computed as `min(1.0, score / 20.0)`. This design intentionally biases toward longer, more specific keywords (e.g., "structural variant" scores 19 points vs. "snp" scoring 3 points), reducing ambiguity when queries contain multiple overlapping terms.

Sources: [genomics_orchestrator.py](Skills/Genomics/orchestrator/genomics_orchestrator.py#L56-L101), [sc_orchestrator.py](Skills/Transcriptomics/orchestrator/sc_orchestrator.py#L51-L98)

## Genomics Skill Landscape

The Genomics Orchestrator routes queries across 10 canonical skills covering the complete bulk sequencing analysis pipeline. Each skill has both a `SKILL.md` manifest and a Python implementation file, enabling both LLM-guided and programmatic invocation. The following table summarizes the full skill catalog with their routing keywords and primary tools.

| Skill | Description | Primary Tools | Key Routing Keywords |

These sub-skills each follow the `SKILL.md` + `examples/` + `usage-guide.md` convention and are individually addressable by the BioKernel's semantic router.

## Specialized AI Agents

Beyond the orchestrator-routed skills, the platform includes 12 **specialized AI agents** that deliver domain-specific intelligence for complex analytical tasks. These agents are distinguished from skills by their use of foundation models, multi-step planning, and autonomous code generation. The following table provides a comparative overview.

| Agent | Domain | Foundation Model | Key Capability | GPU Required |
|-------|--------|-----------------|----------------|--------------|
| **scFoundation Model Agent** | scRNA-seq | scGPT, Geneformer, scBERT, UCE | Cross-species annotation, perturbation prediction | 16GB+ VRAM |
| **CellAgent** | Cell annotation | LLM (multi-provider) | Multi-agent planning, self-correcting code generation | No |
| **BioStudio Alpha SC** | GPU-accelerated scRNA | BioTuring Alpha SC | 10-30× GPU speedup, Blackwell-class acceleration | Blackwell/Hopper GPU |
| **CompBioAgent** | Interactive exploration | LLM + Cellxgene VIP | Natural language querying, web-based visualization | No |
| **CNV Caller Agent** | Cancer genomics | Deep learning segmentation | Somatic/germline CNV, purity/ploidy estimation | No |
| **CRISPR Design Agent** | Genome engineering | DeepCRISPR, CFD scoring | sgRNA selection, off-target evaluation, oligo generation | No |
| **RNA Velocity Agent** | scRNA dynamics | scVelo dynamical, veloVI | Differentiation trajectory prediction, driver gene ID | GPU recommended |
| **Nicheformer Spatial Agent** | Spatial transcriptomics | Nicheformer (53M+ cells) | Spatial niche discovery, zero-shot annotation | 16GB+ VRAM |
| **Epigenomics MethylGPT Agent** | DNA methylation | MethylGPT, DiffuCpG | DMR detection, cancer epigenome profiling | No |
| **PopEVE Variant Predictor** | Variant pathogenicity | PopEVE (Harvard) | VUS resolution, population-aware scoring | No |
| **Cell-Free RNA Agent** | Liquid biopsy | Gradient boosting, neural nets | Cancer detection from cfRNA, tissue deconvolution | No |
| **SIMO Integration Agent** | Spatial multi-omics | Multi-modal VAE, optimal transport | Spatial-epigenomic integration, niche discovery | GPU recommended |

> [!TIP]
> When selecting an agent for a task, start with the orchestrator's routing output to identify the base skill, then evaluate whether the task requires foundation model inference (e.g., cross-species annotation → scFoundation Model Agent) or can be handled by traditional tools (e.g., standard QC → sc-preprocessing). The foundation model agents are computationally expensive and should be reserved for tasks that genuinely benefit from transfer learning.

Sources: [scFoundation Model Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/scFoundation_Model_Agent/SKILL.md#L1-L210), [CellAgent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/Single_Cell/CellAgent/SKILL.md#L1-L69), [BioStudio Alpha SC SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/Single_Cell/BioStudio_Alpha_SC/SKILL.md#L1-L95), [CompBioAgent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/Single_Cell/CompBioAgent/SKILL.md#L1-L67), [CNV Caller Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/CNV_Caller_Agent/SKILL.md#L1-L171), [CRISPR Design Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/CRISPR_Design_Agent/SKILL.md#L1-L72), [RNA Velocity Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/RNA_Velocity_Agent/SKILL.md#L1-L174), [Nicheformer Spatial Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/Nicheformer_Spatial_Agent/SKILL.md#L1-L197), [Epigenomics MethylGPT Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/Epigenomics_MethylGPT_Agent/SKILL.md#L1-L111), [PopEVE Variant Predictor SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/PopEVE_Variant_Predictor_Agent/SKILL.md#L1-L213), [CellFree RNA Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/CellFree_RNA_Agent/SKILL.md#L1-L182), [SIMO Integration Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/SIMO_Multiomics_Integration_Agent/SKILL.md#L1-L178)

## Foundation Model Ecosystem for Single-Cell Analysis

The scFoundation Model Agent serves as the unified gateway to six transformer-based foundation models trained on tens of millions of single-cell profiles. These models share a common architectural paradigm — gene-level tokenization, masked expression prediction pretraining, and attention-based gene interaction modeling — but differ in training data composition, parameter count, and task specialization. The following comparison guides model selection.

| Model | Parameters | Training Data | Best For | Perturbation R² | Annotation Accuracy |
|-------|-----------|---------------|----------|-----------------|-------------------|
| scGPT | 50M | 33M human cells | General purpose, perturbations | 0.87 (Norman 2019) | 93% (Tabula Sapiens) |
| Geneformer | 10M | 30M cells | Chromatin, gene networks | — | 91% (HLCA) |
| scBERT | 20M | 1.2M cells | Cell type annotation | — | — |
| scFoundation | 100M | 50M cells | Large-scale, multi-species | — | — |
| scTab | 15M | 22M cells | Tabular classification | — | — |
| UCE | 100M | 36M cells | Cross-species transfer | — | 85% F1 (Human→Mouse) |

The agent supports five task modes — `annotation`, `perturbation`, `grn_inference`, `integration`, and `embedding` — each with model-specific command-line arguments. For annotation, the workflow accepts a query AnnData object and a reference atlas, generates embeddings for both, and transfers labels via nearest-neighbor matching in the shared embedding space. For perturbation prediction, the model takes a gene knockout specification and produces a counterfactual expression profile. For GRN inference, attention patterns are decomposed into transcription-factor-to-target edge weights.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Input"
        A["AnnData<br/>(.h5ad)"]
    end

    subgraph "Tokenization"
        B["Gene tokenization<br/>+ expression<br/>normalization"]

    subgraph "Foundation Models"
        direction TB
        M1["scGPT<br/>50M params"]

        T5["Cell<br/>Embeddings"]
    end

    subgraph "Ensemble"

    end

    A --> B
    B --> M1
    B --> M2
    B --> M3
    B --> M4
    B --> M5

    M1 --> T1
    M1 --> T2
    M1 --> T3
    M1 --> T4
    M1 --> T5
    M2 --> T1
    M2 --> T2
    M2 --> T3
    M2 --> T4

    M3 --> T1
    M3 --> T2

    T2 --> E
    T3 --> E
    T4 --> E
    T5 --> E
```

> [!TIP]
> Gene coverage is the most common failure mode for foundation model agents. Before invoking any model, verify that the model's training gene set overlaps sufficiently with your dataset's expressed genes. Models trained on human-only data (scGPT, scBERT) will fail silently on mouse data unless you use UCE, which was explicitly designed for cross-species transfer with species-agnostic embeddings.

Sources: [scFoundation Model Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/scFoundation_Model_Agent/SKILL.md#L59-L96), [scFoundation Model Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/scFoundation_Model_Agent/SKILL.md#L146-L178)

## Single-Cell QC Pipeline

The **Single-Cell RNA QC** skill implements a MAD (Median Absolute Deviation) based quality control workflow that serves as the mandatory entry point for all downstream single-cell analyses. It accepts `.h5ad`, 10x `.h5`, or 10x directory inputs, computes mitochondrial and ribosomal gene metrics, applies configurable MAD thresholds for cell filtering, and generates before/after visualization plots alongside a `qc_summary.json` artifact. The workflow is deliberately scoped to QC only — doublet detection and batch correction remain separate skills to enforce modularity and reproducibility.

The QC pipeline is implemented across three modules: `qc_core.py` provides the filtering logic and metric computation, `qc_analysis.py` exposes the CLI interface and orchestrates the workflow, and `qc_plotting.py` generates the standard before/after metric visualizations with threshold overlays. The `reliability` field in the SKILL.md manifest explicitly scores the pipeline against the Scanpy repository (0.90) and the Theis Lab single-cell best-practices playbook (0.88), providing auditable provenance for the MAD-based threshold methodology.

| QC Parameter | Default | Description |
|-------------|---------|-------------|
| `mad_counts` | 5 | MAD multiplier for total counts filter |
| `mad_genes` | 5 | MAD multiplier for gene count filter |
| `mt_threshold` | 20% | Hard mitochondrial percentage ceiling |
| `min_cells` | 3 | Minimum cells expressing a gene |
| `log1p` | true | Apply log1p transform after scaling |

Sources: [Single_Cell_RNA_QC SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/Single_Cell_RNA_QC/SKILL.md#L1-L54), [qc_core.py](Skills/Genomics/Single_Cell_RNA_QC/qc_core.py#L1-L1)

## Spatial and Multi-Omics Agent Integration

The spatial transcriptomics and multi-omics integration agents represent the frontier of the platform's analytical capabilities, bridging single-cell resolution with tissue-level architecture. The **Nicheformer Spatial Agent** leverages a foundation model pretrained on 53 million spatially resolved cells, using a dual-encoder architecture (expression transformer + spatial graph attention) fused via cross-attention to produce spatial-context-aware embeddings. The **SIMO Multiomics Integration Agent** takes a complementary probabilistic approach, using variational autoencoders and optimal transport to align disparate modalities — scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, scMethylation, and CITE-seq protein — onto shared spatial coordinates.

The two agents are designed to interoperate: Nicheformer provides the spatial embedding and niche discovery layer, while SIMO provides the multi-modal alignment and uncertainty quantification. A typical combined workflow first runs SIMO to integrate scATAC-seq chromatin accessibility data with spatial transcriptomics, then feeds the integrated spatial multi-omics object into Nicheformer for spatially-aware niche clustering. The following table summarizes the supported spatial platforms across both agents.

| Platform | Resolution | Cells/Spots | Gene Coverage | Nicheformer | SIMO |
|----------|-----------|-------------|---------------|-------------|------|
| 10x Xenium | Subcellular | >100K | 300-5,000 panel | ✓ | ✓ |
| MERFISH | Subcellular | >1M | 100-10,000 panel | ✓ | ✓ |
| CosMx | Subcellular | >1M | 1,000-6,000 panel | ✓ | ✓ |
| 10x Visium | 55 μm spot | ~5K | Whole transcriptome | ✓ | ✓ |
| 10x Visium HD | 8 μm spot | ~300K | Whole transcriptome | ✓ | ✓ |
| Slide-seq | 10 μm bead | ~60K | Whole transcriptome | ✓ | ✓ |

Sources: [Nicheformer Spatial Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/Nicheformer_Spatial_Agent/SKILL.md#L53-L95), [SIMO Integration Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/SIMO_Multiomics_Integration_Agent/SKILL.md#L48-L110)

## Variant Analysis and Clinical Genomics Agents

Three agents form the clinical genomics axis: the **CNV Caller Agent** for copy number alteration detection, the **PopEVE Variant Predictor** for missense variant pathogenicity scoring, and the **Epigenomics MethylGPT Agent** for DNA methylation analysis. These agents address distinct clinical scenarios but share a common design principle: they augment traditional statistical methods with deep learning models that capture patterns inaccessible to conventional pipelines.

The CNV Caller Agent supports six calling methods (FACETS, ASCAT, CNVkit, GATK CNV, PURPLE, CONICS) and produces allele-specific copy number calls with purity/ploidy estimation. Its AI/ML enhancements focus on three areas: deep learning segmentation for improved breakpoint detection in low-coverage data, sample quality prediction with artifact detection, and GISTIC-style driver prioritization with functional impact scoring. The PopEVE Variant Predictor integrates four feature modules — evolutionary (UniRef90, 250M sequences), structural (AlphaFold2, 200M+ structures), population (gnomAD, 800K+ individuals), and clinical (ClinVar, 100K+ classifications) — achieving an AUROC of 0.95 on ClinVar benchmarks and resolving 45% of VUS cases. The Epigenomics MethylGPT Agent combines a transformer-based foundation model for methylation state prediction with a DiffuCpG generative model for missing data imputation, supporting WGBS, RRBS, and Illumina array (450K, EPIC) platforms.

| Agent | Clinical Application | AI Enhancement | Key Metric |
|-------|---------------------|----------------|------------|
| CNV Caller | Tumor somatic CNV, rare disease germline | DL segmentation, driver prioritization | Purity/ploidy estimation |
| PopEVE | Rare disease VUS resolution | Multi-modal deep learning (evo+struct+pop) | 0.95 AUROC, 45% VUS resolution |
| MethylGPT | Cancer epigenome profiling | Transformer + diffusion imputation | Single-base DMR resolution |

Sources: [CNV Caller Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/CNV_Caller_Agent/SKILL.md#L52-L122), [PopEVE Variant Predictor SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/PopEVE_Variant_Predictor_Agent/SKILL.md#L50-L145), [Epigenomics MethylGPT Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/Epigenomics_MethylGPT_Agent/SKILL.md#L37-L95)

## Liquid Biopsy and Cell-Free RNA

The **Cell-Free RNA Agent** extends the genomics domain into non-invasive diagnostics, analyzing circulating cfRNA from plasma for cancer detection, tissue-of-origin identification, and transcriptomic profiling. Unlike cfDNA-based liquid biopsy (which captures genomic mutations and methylation), cfRNA captures the **active transcriptional state** of source tissues, enabling real-time monitoring of gene expression changes. The agent implements tissue deconvolution using GTEx reference transcriptomes and single-cell atlases, cancer detection via gradient boosting classifiers operating on gene panels, and multi-analyte integration with cfDNA for combined genomic-transcriptomic biomarker panels.

The cfRNA analysis pipeline requires careful attention to pre-analytical variables: sample collection must use EDTA or cell-stabilizing tubes, processing must complete within 4 hours, and hemolysis avoidance is critical since red blood cell lysis introduces confounding transcripts. The agent's cancer detection performance varies by cancer type, with lung cancer achieving AUC 0.80-0.90 using marker panels including XIST and MALAT1, while prostate cancer detection leverages established markers PCA3 and TMPRSS2-ERG.

Sources: [CellFree RNA Agent SKILL.md](Skills/Genomics/CellFree_RNA_Agent/SKILL.md#L38-L145)

## End-to-End Workflow: From Raw Data to Biological Insight

```mermaid
flowchart TB

```
